blocks.content: Opening a TCP connection takes three steps, the three way handshake covered in the previous topic. Closing one cleanly takes four. This topic explains exactly why, and walks through the full close process step by step.
The extra step is not an accident or an inconsistency, it comes directly from a genuine structural fact about TCP connections that is easy to miss if you have not looked closely.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784014301259-410944579.png
blocks.alt: The full four way close: FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK, each side closing its own direction independently

blocks.content: 1. Why Closing Needs More Steps Than Opening
blocks.text: 1. Why Closing Needs More Steps Than Opening

blocks.content: A TCP connection is actually two independent, separate data streams running in opposite directions at once, client to server and server to client. Each direction has to be closed independently, since one side might genuinely still have more data left to send even after the other side is completely finished.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784014303228-563682719.png
blocks.alt: A TCP connection is really two independent streams, one in each direction, each closing on its own schedule

blocks.title: The entire reason for the extra step
blocks.content: This is the whole explanation in one sentence: opening only needs to establish one shared agreement, but closing needs each of the two independent directions to be shut down on its own, which is exactly what turns three steps into four.
2. Step One: FIN From the Initiator
blocks.text: 2. Step One: FIN From the Initiator

blocks.content: The side that wants to close sends a segment with the FIN flag set. This says, plainly, I have no more data to send from my side. It does not say anything at all about the other direction of the connection.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784014304971-375700068.png
blocks.alt: Step one: the initiating side sends FIN, announcing it has no more data to send

blocks.content: 3. Step Two: ACK From the Other Side
blocks.text: 3. Step Two: ACK From the Other Side

blocks.content: The receiving side acknowledges the FIN, confirming it heard the close request. This is genuinely important to get right: this ACK does NOT mean the other side own direction is closed too. It may still have more data of its own left to send back.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784014306636-619298987.png
blocks.alt: Step two: the other side acknowledges the FIN, but its own direction can stay open

blocks.content: 4. Steps Three and Four: The Other Side Closes Too
blocks.text: 4. Steps Three and Four: The Other Side Closes Too

blocks.content: Once the second side has genuinely finished sending everything it needs to send, it sends its own FIN, now saying, I also have no more data to send. The original initiator acknowledges this second FIN, and only at this point is the connection considered fully, completely closed on both sides.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784014308346-89566816.png
blocks.alt: Steps three and four: the second side sends its own FIN once ready, and the initiator sends the final ACK

5. When Steps Two and Three Collapse Into One
blocks.text: 5. When Steps Two and Three Collapse Into One

blocks.content: In some cases, if the second side happens to already be ready to close at the exact moment it acknowledges the first FIN, its ACK and its own FIN can be combined into a single segment. This can make the close look like three steps instead of four in practice, though conceptually it is still four distinct actions, two of them just happened to travel together.
6. TIME WAIT: A Genuinely Important, Often Confusing State
blocks.text: 6. TIME WAIT: A Genuinely Important, Often Confusing State

blocks.content: After sending the final ACK, the side that sent it does not immediately discard everything about the connection. It waits in a special TIME WAIT state for a period of time before fully closing. This exists specifically in case that final ACK was lost, if the connection information were already gone, a resent FIN from the other side would have nowhere to go.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784014309883-951920805.png
blocks.alt: TIME WAIT exists specifically to handle the case where the final ACK itself gets lost along the way

blocks.content: 7. Why TIME WAIT Can Actually Cause Real Problems
blocks.text: 7. Why TIME WAIT Can Actually Cause Real Problems

blocks.content: A server handling a very high volume of short lived connections can accumulate a large number of connections sitting in TIME WAIT at once, since each one lingers for a real period of time before fully clearing. This is a genuinely well known practical issue in high traffic server design, worth knowing by name even without needing every low level tuning detail.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784014312750-508460928.png
blocks.alt: A high volume server can accumulate many connections in TIME WAIT simultaneously, a real, well known scaling concern

blocks.content: 8. Opening Versus Closing, Side by Side
blocks.text: 8. Opening Versus Closing, Side by Side

blocks.content: Ending a phone call is not always simultaneous. One person might say, I am done talking now, but the other person still has one more thing to say before they are also ready to hang up. Only once BOTH people have said their final piece does the call actually end. That is the four way close in miniature.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784014314978-128284492.png
blocks.alt: Opening needs three steps since nothing exists yet; closing needs four since two independent directions must each close on their own

9. A Worked Example: One Side Finishes Before the Other
blocks.text: 9. A Worked Example: One Side Finishes Before the Other

blocks.content: A client finishes sending its request and sends FIN. The server is still streaming back the remainder of a large response, so it acknowledges the client FIN immediately, but does not send its own FIN until it has genuinely finished sending everything. Only then does the connection fully close, exactly reflecting that the two directions really did finish at different times.

blocks.title: A quick contrast: RST
blocks.content: Unlike this graceful four step close, a RST segment aborts a connection immediately and ungracefully, typically used when something has genuinely gone wrong rather than a normal, healthy close. Worth knowing this alternate, non graceful path exists.
10. Common Mistakes and Key Takeaways

["Assuming both directions of a TCP connection always close simultaneously, when they are genuinely independent and can close at different times.","Confusing TIME WAIT as something that indicates a problem, when it is a normal, deliberate part of a healthy close, just one that can accumulate at high scale.","A TCP connection is really two independent streams that close separately.","The four steps are FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK, and steps two and three can sometimes combine.","TIME WAIT protects against a lost final ACK, but can accumulate under heavy short lived connection load.","RST is a separate, abrupt, non graceful way a connection can end."]
items: Assuming both directions of a TCP connection always close simultaneously, when they are genuinely independent and can close at different times.
Confusing TIME WAIT as something that indicates a problem, when it is a normal, deliberate part of a healthy close, just one that can accumulate at high scale.
A TCP connection is really two independent streams that close separately.
The four steps are FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK, and steps two and three can sometimes combine.
TIME WAIT protects against a lost final ACK, but can accumulate under heavy short lived connection load.
RST is a separate, abrupt, non graceful way a connection can end.
